name: The Humane League: policy, new commitments, volunteers and the Open Wing Alliance
beneficiaries_note: Our build: animals, by share of the result at the defaults. New corporate commitments 'around the world' (48%) and the Open Wing Alliance's wins abroad (8%) spread by world population; grassroots pressure on switches at companies THL pressed itself (38%), 55% US by ACE's hens in the engaged US and global supply chains (135 and 114 million); state-law defence and the Animal Policy Alliance in the US (6%). A judgment.
summary: The Humane League's other programmes cost about $5.2 million in 2025, its programme spending less its grants and its accountability campaigns (two other lines): defending US state cage-free and crate-free laws against a federal override and supporting the Animal Policy Alliance's local campaigns, winning new corporate cage-free commitments (four companies, 1.6 million hens), running the Open Wing Alliance (its team, summits, trainings and Fair and Fowl report, credited with a share of the members' 216 new cage-free policies, 16 restored pledges and 18 broiler policies abroad), and mobilising volunteers and supporters to press companies to keep their commitments (a share of the 5.5 million hens out of cages at companies THL pressed itself). The money is split by THL's annual report and ACE's 2024 breakdown, and each part is built from THL's own counts and the site's shared figures per hen, broiler, sow and meal; every branch is discounted for missing data. Past wins count at THL's own next-dollar figure. The biggest uncertainties are how much grassroots pressure adds to what companies would do anyway, THL's share among the groups behind its new commitments, the hens behind the Alliance's average new policy, and whether the 2025 opposition changed the chance that Congress overrides the state laws (one event, drawn as happens or doesn't, so the defence counts mainly at high risk settings).

sections.title: Your dollar's share

New commitments, the Open Wing Alliance and volunteers, 2025
rows.explainer: The rest of the money: corporate engagement for new commitments, the Open Wing Alliance's running, and grassroots mobilisation with its communications.

rows.label: Campaigns for new corporate commitments, 2025
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The annual report's US Public Policy & Corporate Engagement ($2.50 million, $2.54 million on the Form 990's total) less ACE's smaller accountability block ($1.65 million in 2025 prices) and the policy work above leaves about $0.2 million; global staff winning commitments abroad add some. Four new commitments in 2025 (1.6 million hens).

rows.label: THL's own spending on running the alliance (staff, trainings, Fair and Fowl)
rows.explainer: Our judgment: THL's annual report (p. 17: Global Programs $5,204,000 with the THL UK grant; Education & Mobilization $4,664,000; US Public Policy & Corporate Engagement $2,498,000; OWA & APA Grants $1,991,000) leaves $3.05 million of global programmes after the THL UK grant, which ACE's global accountability block ($1.65 million in 2025 prices) and the alliance's running fill: about $1.5 million. ACE treats the Open Wing Alliance's coordination as paths of its own, outside cage-free accountability, so it is in THL's other programmes: the alliance's team, four regional summits, trainings (four Campaign Accelerators, 13 webinars, 19 campaign chats, 21 action parties), mentorship (27 mentees) and the Fair and Fowl report. The same judgment in THL's grants and other-programmes models.

rows.label: Volunteers, grassroots mobilisation and their communications, 2025
rows.explainer: The remainder, mostly the annual report's Education & Mobilization ($4.66 million): organising THL's volunteers and supporters (about 1,300 changemakers, 6,180 actions and 1.48 million messages in 2025), protests, investigations and the communications that carry them, as far as ACE's accountability costs leave them out. Never below zero.

rows.label: Overhead multiplier (total ÷ programme expenses)
rows.explainer: Spreads management and fundraising over programmes in proportion to their cost, as GiveWell and ACE do.

rows.explainer: Our judgment: the commitments are 'around the world'; US and most non-European hens are in battery cages, the EU's in enriched ones. The share picks the shared SADs figure (battery-cage hens, 2024 SADs; enriched, 2025 SADs).

The grants line's model's judgment.

rows.label: Hens under the Alliance members' accountability wins (REWE and 15 others)
rows.explainer: REWE's hens not yet cage-free and the other 15 wins of the Fair and Fowl report, the grants line's pool. It also stands in for the year's switches at the companies the members pressed, which are taken out of THL's count below so the same hens count in one pool only.

rows.label: Of those, UK hens switched at companies THL UK pressed (credited in the grants line)
rows.explainer: Our judgment. THL's count is of hens at the companies it and the Alliance pressed, so its UK part is the switches at THL UK's engaged companies, not the whole country's change: ACE's sheet puts those companies' supply chains at 2.55 million hens, most already compliant. The high end is the UK's whole change in 2025 (82.7% against 78.6% cage-free of about 45 million hens, Our World in Data and the British Egg Information Service). THL UK is a separate charity THL funds by a grant, so these switches are credited in the grants line (as a share of the UK's whole change) and taken out here.

rows.label: New cage-free policies won by Open Wing Alliance members, 2025

source.title: Open Wing Alliance, 2025 end-of-year review (The Humane League, 18 February 2026)
source.quote: 216 new cage-free policies are now secured, helping egg-laying hens out of cages

rows.explainer: The alliance's count for 2025 (with 18 broiler policies implemented, the 990's '234 new corporate commitments for chickens', more than 60 in Africa).

rows.label: Share of the alliance's wins outside the US
rows.explainer: Our judgment. The alliance's 82 members work in 72 countries; THL's own new US commitments were four ('spare 1.6 million hens around the world', 990 Part III), and the review's named wins are in Ghana, Indonesia, Latvia and Europe. US wins belong to THL's own campaigns (another line), so they are taken out here and from the staff count below alike.

rows.label: Hens a year covered by an average new policy
rows.explainer: Our judgment: no tracker gives hens for the 216 policies. Anchors: the largest named, Agro Innova in Ghana, distributes about 15 million eggs a month (about 600,000 hens at some 300 eggs a hen-year); THL's four new commitments covered 1.6 million hens (large US and European firms); most of the alliance's policies are hotels, bakeries, restaurants and regional producers with a few thousand hens each. A skewed mix averages about 10,000. The grants line's model's judgment.

rows.label: Share of those hens not yet cage-free when the policy was won
rows.explainer: Our judgment: outside the EU, UK and US nearly all hens are caged (Welfare Footprint's country compilation in Our World in Data's cage-free series), but some companies pledge when they already buy some cage-free eggs.

rows.label: Hens a year under the Alliance's new policies abroad, not yet cage-free
rows.explainer: The grants line's pool. Everything the policies cover is counted; whether companies keep them is the shared rate of pledges kept.

rows.label: Share of the hens abroad in enriched rather than battery cages
rows.explainer: Our judgment, anchored on Schedule F: Europe outside the UK took $426,310 of the $1.69 million of listed grants abroad (25%), and the EU has used enriched cages since 2012; Africa, Latin America and Asia use battery cages. Policies in Europe are fewer per dollar than in the Global South, hence 20%.

rows.explainer: Our judgment: the review names none of the 18. A European retailer's or food-service firm's own-brand chicken runs to millions of birds a year, a restaurant chain's to tens of thousands; the median policy is assumed mid-sized.

SADs averted per hen-year, new commitments
rows.explainer: The shared figures for a hen moved from a battery cage (2024 SADs) or an enriched cage (2025 SADs) to an aviary, mixed by the share above. The species step converts the two versions separately.

rows.explainer: The shared figures, battery (2024 SADs) and enriched (2025 SADs), mixed by the share in enriched cages.

rows.explainer: Hens that would go back to battery cages if the laws fell (US cages are battery cages).

rows.label: SADs averted per animal-year, average of the branches (for reading only)
rows.formula: (new_sads_per_hen_year * new_hens * new_share_not_compliant + owa_sads_per_hen_year * (owanew_hens + owaacc_hens) + owabcc_sads_per_broiler * owabcc_broilers + vol_sads_per_hen_year * (vol_hens_switched - owaacc_hens - uk_switches_in_count) + def_sads_per_hen_year * def_hens + def_sads_per_sow_year * def_sows) / (new_hens * new_share_not_compliant + owanew_hens + owaacc_hens + owabcc_broilers + vol_hens_switched - owaacc_hens - uk_switches_in_count + def_hens + def_sows)
rows.explainer: Animal-weighted average of the shared figures the branches use, for reading only; each branch uses its own.

rows.label: Share of the animals under the laws that would go back into cages within the years counted if the laws fell
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the same as the grants line's model: in-state housing laws and company pledges would keep most cage-free and crate-free supply, and barns already built rarely go back to cages; replacement barns, buyers without pledges and price pressure after bird flu would bring some back.

rows.label: Chance a federal override of the state laws passes without the coalition's 2025 opposition

source.title: The Humane League, Animal Policy Alliance year in review (February 2026)
source.quote: By the end of the year, more than 200 members of Congress had signed letters opposing the EATS language

rows.explainer: Our judgment, the same as the grants line's model. The EATS Act's language and the 'Save Our Bacon' Act were in the House Farm Bill drafts of 2024-25 and the Department of Justice sued California over Proposition 12 in 2025; the coalition (Humane World for Animals, the ASPCA, THL and the Alliance's groups) gathered letters from more than 200 members of Congress against them (228, the annual report says, p. 6). Without that opposition we put an override in the next Farm Bill at 30%. One event, drawn as happens or doesn't.

rows.label: Chance it passes with the coalition's 2025 opposition
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the same as the grants line's model: the year's opposition takes about 5 points off (a sixth of the risk). Research on lobbying finds most campaigns change nothing (Baumgartner and colleagues, 2009); organised constituent contact moved legislators' support by about 12 points in a field experiment (Bergan and Cole, 2015). Drawn together with the chance without it.

rows.label: Fall in production per meal not bought
rows.explainer: The site's one production response for diet change.

rows.label: Suffering in a US meal relative to the reference meal
rows.explainer: The site's US figure (docs/normalization.md 2.9): ACE's 2025 meal estimates put a US meal at 1.5 times the global one (0.75-3); the shared per-meal figure is a Latin American canteen meal.

rows.label: SADs averted per meal replaced
Share of new commitments that will later need accountability pressure
rows.explainer: Our judgment, the grants line's model's: the trackers and the Fair and Fowl report follow the larger companies, so about half the hens under a new pledge later get pressed. Later pressure is credited to later years' accountability, so a new commitment is credited only with what that pressure won't add (the template's recipe).

rows.label: Share of switches under pressed commitments that wouldn't have come yet without the pressure
rows.explainer: Our judgment, one question per switch: would it have come this year anyway? The anchor, pressed pledges kept at 92% (the Open Wing Alliance's tracker, 2025 Fair and Fowl report) against 77% for all due cage-free pledges (the site's shared rate), gives (0.92 - 0.77) / 0.92, about 0.16, for an average pressed pledge. The switches credited here come from companies that had stalled or gone silent (Subway, Walmart, Ahold Delhaize; REWE dropped its deadline), where pressure matters more than for a pledge already on track (THL UK's switches under passed UK deadlines take 0.2), so 0.3 (0.1-0.6). Each switch credited counts the shared years.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (how far the reach and effect above can be trusted)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, about the validity of the counts only (that the outcome isn't measured is the missing-data step): THL's count of hens under the four companies' commitments is its own, from the companies' egg volumes, and 'around the world' is unchecked.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (how far the reach and effect above can be trusted)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, about the validity of the counts only (that the outcome isn't measured is the missing-data step): THL's count of 7.5 million hens spared is its own and may include switches at companies it didn't press.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (how far the reach and effect above can be trusted)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, about the validity of the counts only (that the outcome isn't measured is the missing-data step): the hens are taken by population share, and some of those states' supply is under in-state housing laws an override wouldn't touch (as in the grants line's model of THL, 0.9).

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (how far the reach and effect above can be trusted)
rows.explainer: Our judgment, about the validity of the counts only (that the outcome isn't measured is the missing-data step): THL's count of 10 'major' wins is its own, and some wins (a foie gras ban, a rabbit-farm proposal dropped) fit the per-meal figure loosely.

rows.label: Share of the new commitments' gain not credited to later pressure
rows.explainer: Whether the commitments would have come anyway is the years counted (a new commitment counts the shared years); what later accountability adds is credited there.

rows.label: Share of the switches that wouldn't have come yet without the pressure
What would have happened anyway (in the two chances above)
rows.explainer: 1: the chance of an override with and without the coalition's work already says what would have happened anyway.

rows.label: What would have happened anyway (in the years counted)
rows.explainer: 1: a win that would have come later anyway is counted for the shared years only (one question per adjustment, Convention 5).

Side effect: wider gains from won commitments and laws, as a share of the animals' gain
rows.explainer: Our judgment. Won commitments and defended laws push producers to convert barns that also supply buyers without a commitment and make further laws easier; investigations and protests reach the public (the 2025 egg-farm investigation reached 451 media outlets). Range 0-30%.

rows.label: Side effect: caged eggs and crated pork sold elsewhere, as a share of the animals' gain
rows.explainer: Our judgment. When a buyer or a state stops taking caged eggs, some of those eggs are sold to other buyers for a while, so fewer hens leave cages than the commitment covers; dearer cage-free eggs move a few buyers to chicken meat (more animals per calorie), while fewer eggs bought offsets part. A harm, so negative. Range 0 to -25%.
